questions.q: Why did the Event Horizon Telescope need to be almost as wide as the Earth?
questions.do: Under Make it sharper, press Radio (1.3 mm), then try 10 m telescope, VLA (36 km) and EHT (10,700 km). Read Blur ÷ ring.
questions.a: Sharpness is about 1.22 × wavelength ÷ telescope width. At 1.3 mm even the 36 km VLA blurs about 9,000 µas, hundreds of times bigger than the 42 µas ring. Only a 10,700 km telescope gets the blur down to about 31 µas, smaller than the ring, so the dark middle shows.

questions.q: Using Einstein's formula, how big should the shadow of Sgr A* look, and does it match the picture?
questions.do: In How big is the shadow?, press Sgr A* and read Computed shadow and Measured ring.
questions.a: With 4.3 million Suns at 8.3 kpc, the formula gives about 53 µas. The EHT measured 51.8 ± 2.3 µas, so it matches within the error.

questions.q: M87* is about 1,500 times heavier than Sgr A*. Why do the two rings look almost the same size?
questions.do: Switch between M87* and Sgr A* in How big is the shadow? and read the verdict below the chart.
questions.a: M87 is also about 2,000 times farther away. The shadow's size grows with mass but its angle shrinks with distance, so the two effects almost cancel: about 40 µas against about 53 µas.

questions.q: How long would it take to send the 5 petabytes from 2017 over a 100 Mbit/s home connection?
questions.do: In Data by aeroplane, press Home broadband (100 Mbit/s) and read Time to move it all.
questions.a: About 12.7 years, running non-stop. Flying about 1,000 hard drives took days, which is why the data travelled by aeroplane to MIT Haystack and Bonn.

questions.q: When were the first pictures of M87* and Sgr A* shown to the world, and which one came first?
questions.a: M87* came first, on 10 April 2019. Sgr A*, the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy, followed on 12 May 2022. Both used data recorded in April 2017.
